name: The Microphones
label: K
lede: A record-store clerk in Anacortes, a studio in Olympia, and one guy running his guitar through the microphone jack of a thrift-store cassette deck. Then he changed the name, and twenty years later he changed it back.

eras.title: A back room at The Business
eras.text: Phil Elverum is a teenager clerking at an Anacortes record store and recording in its back room. By 1998 he has moved to Olympia, and the town's label owner has noticed.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Microphones · Wikipedia: Phil Elverum · Wikipedia: Tests (album)
years.h: A clerk at The Business starts recording in the back room
years.p: Phil Elverum works at the Anacortes record store The Business and uses its back room as a studio. Owner Bret Lunsford releases two Microphones cassettes on his Knw-Yr-Own label: Microphone and Wires and Cords.
years.xp:
Elverum was also drumming for Lunsford's band D+ around the same time. His own account is that the record store was his entry point to alternative music.

Wikipedia says the Tests tapes were recorded at The Business while he worked there, and that the 1998 CD later compiled that material with newer recordings. The Business is also where he did his high-school recording experiments, per Wikipedia's Don't Wake Me Up article.

years.h: Elverum moves to Olympia and lands on Calvin Johnson's radar
years.p: He enrolls at Evergreen State College, then puts the music scene ahead of school. [[Calvin Johnson|cac7a688-14a8-46c3-8fc8-11cca866677c]], who runs K Records, starts recording him at his Dub Narcotic studio.

years.h: Tests on Elsinor: cassette leftovers plus the first Dub Narcotic sessions
years.p: The CD compiles material from the Anacortes cassettes with new recordings made in Olympia. It is the Microphones' first full-length. The 7-inch "Bass Drum Dream" comes out on Up Records the same year.
years.xp: Per Wikipedia, Tests began as a Knw-Yr-Own cassette and took its CD form on Elsinor Records. The same page says P.W. Elverum & Sun later reissued the cassette in an edition of 20 for Record Store Day 2011, sold at The Business.

eras.title: K Records signs the kid
eras.text: Three records in two years on K, recorded in Calvin Johnson's studio with a rotating cast of friends. Everything is on 16-track tape, which means no do-overs.

years.src: Wikipedia: Don't Wake Me Up (album) · Wikipedia: The Microphones
years.h: Don't Wake Me Up: fifteen tracks, one wall of mud
years.p: Elverum was 20 when he finished recording it in a warehouse-sized Olympia room. Mirah, Khaela Maricich, Bronwyn Holm and Calvin Johnson sing on it.
years.xp:
Recording ran from April 1998 to March 1999 at Dub Narcotic in Olympia and at The Business in Anacortes. Pitchfork's Ryan Schreiber praised the muddy production and how the 15 tracks blend into one piece.

Wikipedia's article says the record gave K Records a new sense of what a K release could sound like, and gave Elverum his first real audience.

years.h: [[Mirah|e4c226f2-ba57-483f-be6b-3391112244b8]] tours the US and Canada with the Microphones
years.p: Elverum had invited her to add guitar and vocals, and she played on Don't Wake Me Up and Window. He co-produced her 2000 debut, You Think It's Like This but Really It's Like This.

years.h: Sessions for The Glow Pt. 2 begin at Dub Narcotic
years.p: Recording runs to March 23, 2001, mostly early mornings on 16-track tape. Elverum's distortion comes from running a guitar through the mic input of a thrift-store cassette deck, out the headphone jack and into an amp.
years.xp:
Wikipedia credits [[Karl Blau|688d2d9d-8f49-4187-b558-2c961c699ab1]] as engineer and drum machine operator and [[Khaela Maricich|07d0cdc9-6e87-4645-ba65-a042961c6e7c]] as engineer and vocalist. It says the end of her relationship with Elverum shaped the album's themes, and that Mirah told him in the studio it was going to be something special.

The cover art comes from a 1933–34 Dutch cookbook, Calvé-Delft's Winterboekje. Elverum has named extreme metal, ambient music and Twin Peaks among the influences, per Wikipedia.

years.src: Wikipedia: It Was Hot, We Stayed in the Water · Wikipedia: Karl Blau
years.h: It Was Hot, We Stayed in the Water arrives on K
years.p: It was recorded at Dub Narcotic between September 1999 and March 2000. Pitchfork gave it 9.2 and ranked it seventh on its Top 20 Albums of 2000.
years.xp:
Khaela Maricich wrote the song "(Something)" and Mirah sings guest vocals on "Ice". Karl Blau, an Anacortes musician on the Knw-Yr-Own side of K, also worked on it and has a song titled after him.

Elverum said analog tape gave him a technological reason for charismatic sloppiness: re-recording a take was impractical.

eras.title: From The Glow to Mount Eerie
eras.text: The record everyone names, then a five-song climb up a mountain, a winter in Norway, and a new name.

years.h: The Glow Pt. 2 comes out: 66 minutes, sloppy on purpose
years.p: Pitchfork gave it 9.2 on release and 9.3 for the 2008 reissue. It is the record most people mean when they say Microphones.
years.xp:
The album is stereo throughout, and its sprawl and noise took it from a K release to a reference point: Wikipedia lists Lil Peep, who sampled three tracks, plus Sylvan Esso, Kevin Morby and Wild Nothing's Jack Tatum among artists it influenced. The Guardian called it "a millennial Daydream Nation" in 2013.

Elverum has pushed back on the canon talk. Wikipedia quotes him saying the idea that albums are good, bad or essential is a total myth. It also notes K Records kept poor records, so the record's sales were never counted.

years.h: Song Islands collects the singles and strays
years.p: Twenty-one tracks from 1998 to 2002, including "Bass Drum Dream" and "The Glow, Pt. 4". Pitchfork gave it 7.2.
years.xp: It carries the K Records and P.W. Elverum & Sun credits (ELV 030), one of the first releases with Elverum's own imprint name on it.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Microphones · Wikipedia: Mount Eerie (album)
years.h: A tour, then a winter in a Norwegian log cabin
years.p: After the Paper Opera Tour of Europe and North America, Elverum toured solo as "I Will Move Away Forever and Never Come Back Ever". He spent winter 2002–03 in a cabin in Kjerringøy, Norway.
years.xp: Wikipedia says he moved out of his Olympia house after recording finished and wrote the songs that became Dawn (2008) in Norway.

years.h: Mount Eerie: five tracks, one 17-minute opener, one mountain
years.p: The album follows a climb up Mount Erie on Fidalgo Island, from womb to death, with different vocal characters. Pitchfork rated it 8.9 and Best New Music.
years.xp: It was recorded November 2001 to June 2002 at Dub Narcotic, with two sections done elsewhere: Kyle Field's "Big Black Death" and Karl Blau's "Wind / Vultures" at Quatro-Syncho in Trafton Lake, Washington. It came out in Japan on 7.e.p. on December 12, 2002 before the US release on K.

years.h: Japan tour with Calvin Johnson, Kyle Field and Moools
years.p: The tour produced Live in Japan, which K released in early 2004.

q: The Microphones was completed, or at least at a good stopping point.
years.src: Wikipedia: Mount Eerie · Wikipedia: Phil Elverum
years.h: Elverum stops using the Microphones name
years.p: He starts recording as Mount Eerie, named for the hill he grew up under, and treats it as a new project rather than a rename.
years.xp:
Elverum's line, as reported on Wikipedia: Mount Eerie is a new project, and the Microphones was completed, or at least at a good stopping point.

He later described both names as one progression. Wikipedia counts the Microphones years as 1996–2003.

eras.title: Reissues, and a different kind of record
eras.text: Elverum records as Mount Eerie and presses the old Microphones records himself. Then a death in his family changes what he records.

years.h: The Glow Pt. 2 returns as a double LP on his own label
years.p: Four Microphones studio albums are remastered and reissued on P.W. Elverum & Sun, the label he founded in 2004 to press, package and ship his own records.

years.src: Wikipedia: A Crow Looked at Me · Wikipedia: Geneviève Castrée
years.h: A Crow Looked at Me, recorded in the room where his wife died
years.p: Geneviève Castrée died of pancreatic cancer on July 9, 2016. Elverum recorded the album between August and December in their Anacortes house.
years.xp:
Per Wikipedia he used one microphone, an acoustic guitar and some of her instruments, and chose the room so it would not be defined only by her final days. The New York Times' Jon Caramanica wrote that songwriting seemed too precise a word for it.

Elverum and Castrée had married in 2004 and had one child, born in 2015.

eras.title: Microphones in 2020
eras.text: Elverum plays a hometown show as the Microphones, then makes one record about the name.

years.p: Elverum plays the hometown show with D+, Black Belt Eagle Scout and Little Wings on the bill.

years.h: Microphones in 2020: one 44:44 song about being Phil Elverum
years.p: He announced it June 16 and recorded it between May 2019 and May 2020. Pitchfork gave it 8.5 and Best New Music.
years.xp:
It opens with about seven minutes of instrumental, two double-tracked chords, before speak-singing, drums, bass, organ, electric guitar and piano arrive. Wikipedia says it looks back at his career and includes a nod to The Glow Pt. 2.

He left it off Spotify as a protest against the streaming business model, per Wikipedia. Metacritic listed 87 from seven reviews.

years.h: Completely Everything, 1996–2021 announced as the last Microphones release
years.p: Elverum announced a box set gathering the whole run, and said it would be the final Microphones release, per Wikipedia.
years.xp: Wikipedia says he played the new album live in limited dates in 2021 and 2022 before putting the name away again.
